essays.title: if (document.layers): the web forks in two
essays.description: In 1997 Netscape and Microsoft each invented their own model of a web page. Everyone wrote every effect twice, and the way it ended explains a lot about how the web still works.
unverified: That the "Best viewed with" buttons were usually 88 by 31 pixels. The buttons are well documented; I did not open a source for the size.
The mention of Dynamic Drive as a source of copy-and-paste scripts. Its site would not load when this was checked.
Why the two browsers exposed such different models. The engine explanation is my best guess, and the essay says so.

essays.title: Where did all the old web developers go?
essays.description: Around 2008 nobody writing JavaScript seemed to be over 40, and the industry spent a decade arguing about why. The answer was arithmetic, and the same arithmetic is running again.
unverified: Vivek Wadhwa's 2010 TechCrunch piece and the original 2009 "Plan B" essay are named from secondary references. I did not open either directly.
The Stanford and ADP employment figures are quoted from SoftwareSeni's summary, not from the study itself.
The CNBC figure on senior job postings is quoted from Fullstack's summary of CNBC's reporting.
That the staff and principal engineering track spread through the 2010s is my reading, not a sourced claim.

essays.title: getYear() and the year 19100
essays.description: One small Date method returned 100, 2000 or 100 again for the year 2000 depending on the browser, got fixed three different ways, and is still in every browser today.
unverified: The January 2000 sightings of "19100" (the US Naval Observatory, Meteo-France, the Gore campaign site) rest on Wikipedia's Year 2000 problem article, not on the original news reports.
Internet Explorer 9's return to "year minus 1900" in standards mode rests on one reference page.
JDK 1.1 is dated only to February 1997, because sources disagree on the day.
Whether Navigator 4.0 to 4.05 returned 100 or 2000 could not be pinned down, so the essay speaks only about 4.06 and later.
Why Navigator 3 changed the method is my guess, and is marked as one.

essays.title: jQuery 1.0: what $ really replaced
essays.description: jQuery 1.0 shipped in August 2006 with a dollar sign borrowed from another library, and replaced a folder of copy-pasted fixes that its own author had been winning contests with.
unverified: When the "write less, do more" slogan first appeared. It is sourced only to Wikipedia's citation of the jquery.com page title.
The date of the first release. The jQuery project says January 14, 2006; John Resig's own write-up implies the 15th. The essay reports both.
Whether the jquery-1.0.js file on the jQuery CDN is identical to the one released on August 26, 2006. Its header carries an October 2006 revision date.
Why jQuery 1.3.2 used querySelectorAll only for document-rooted queries is my inference.
John Resig's age at the time comes from Wikipedia.

essays.title: View Source was the school
essays.description: For about fifteen years the web trained its own workforce through one menu item that showed how any page was made, and then the pages stopped being readable.
unverified: Netscape's exact menu labels and keyboard shortcut for viewing source. The essay says only that the name varied by browser and year.
Tim O'Reilly's essay is linked in its print view, because the canonical page refused to load.
That the Firefox bug reporter copied the script from a page's source is an inference, and is worded as one.
Why Internet Explorer opened source in Notepad rests on a single 2008 Microsoft blog post.

essays.title: Firebug: the first look inside the page
essays.description: In January 2006 one developer uploaded a few days of code as a Firefox add-on, and within a few years every browser had copied its panels, its F12 key and its console.log.
unverified: Joe Hewitt's own 2006 blog posts. His site is down, so his words are quoted only as they appear in Mozilla Hacks and a FOSDEM interview.
The January 12, 2006 announcement date comes from Jay Hoffmann's history of the web, and is flagged in the text.
That F12 as the developer-tools key began with Firebug 0.2.3 rests on Wikipedia, and is attributed to it.
The Firebug 1.1 source listings come from a third-party mirror, which the essay names.

essays.title: XMLHttpRequest: six years waiting for a name
essays.description: Microsoft shipped the object behind every web application in 1999, under a name its author calls an excuse. Almost nobody used it until a designer's 2005 essay called the technique Ajax.
unverified: Almost everything about how XMLHTTP was written and shipped rests on one account, Alex Hopmann's. He gives no date for the weekend, the naming or the security review beyond starting the webmail work "probably sometime in late 1998", and his page shows no original publication date.
Jesse James Garrett's essay is linked as a saved copy of its print view, because Adaptive Path's own site would not load.

The dates for Mozilla, Safari 1.2 and Opera 8.0 support come from Wikipedia, as do Oddpost's 2002 opening and the release months of Internet Explorer 5 and 7. Wikipedia's XMLHttpRequest article also dates the idea to 2000, which contradicts Hopmann; I followed Hopmann.
Jay Hoffmann's history of the web says XMLHTTP was added to replace Java components that Outlook Web Access had relied on. Hopmann does not mention this, so I left it out.

How little the object was used before 2004 is hard to measure. Aaron Swartz wrote that nobody he knew used it, but Hopmann says the approach was already doing well by 2000 to 2002, and it was common on corporate intranets.
Google's two blog posts are linked for their dates only. Whether Google Maps used XMLHttpRequest or hidden frames at launch is disputed in the comments on Swartz's post, so the essay does not say.

That XMLHTTP sitting behind ActiveX held back public sites, that Prototype's wrapper kept most developers from typing the constructor, and that the missing name mattered as much as I say, are my own readings.

essays.title: The webmaster: a mailbox that became a job
essays.description: "Webmaster" was coined as a mail alias on a style page, grew into the title for whoever ran the whole site, and faded, while the address in the footer link outlived the job.
unverified: That "webmaster" was coined on the etiquette page rests on Tim Berners-Lee's own note on that page. The 1993 date is my inference from a November 1992 snapshot without the word and Merriam-Webster's first-use year.
That the W3C folder named MailArchive/webmaster holds mail sent to the webmaster address is my reading of its name and of the greeting in one message. The archive itself does not say.
The 1996 Web Week survey is quoted from an undated Princeton Review career profile. I could not find the survey itself, and Georgia Tech's webmaster surveys from the same years would not load.
Louise Addis as the first webmaster, and the reasons the role faded, rest on one secondary source, Jay Hoffmann's history.
Google's 2008 "Webmaster Team" and webmaster job ladder rest on one person's blog post.
Microsoft's advisory on the live.fi certificate does not name the mailbox that was registered, so the essay does not either.
That address harvesting drove webmasters to scripts and forms is supported only by Wikipedia and by RFC 2142's warning. The FTC's 2002 study of harvesting would not load, so it is not cited.
The four forces behind the one-person job, and the comparison of the server administrator with an on-call rotation, are my own readings.

essays.title: The IE6 funeral: campaigning to kill a browser
essays.description: In March 2010 a Denver web shop buried Internet Explorer 6 in a pine coffin and Microsoft sent flowers. The browser had a fifth of the market that night, and what finally ended it was not persuasion.
unverified: The card's exact wording. I quote TechCrunch's version; Computerworld printed it slightly differently ("See you at MIX where we'll show..."). Attendance also varies, from "around a hundred" to "between 80 and 100".

I did not open ie6funeral.com or the original 37signals, Digg, IE6 No More and Windows blog posts (those I tried would not load), so the obituary, the 37signals notice, the Digg figures and Roger Capriotti's words are quoted from press coverage and other blogs that reproduced them.
The Digg poll result. Eric Lawrence's post adds two answers to get 69% who could not upgrade, while TechCrunch reported 77%. The poll was self-selected either way.
Everything about the YouTube banner's origin and effect rests on Chris Zacharias's own account, written ten years later, including the claim that YouTube's IE6 audience halved in a month.
The "Retiring IE6" post is signed only "Eric". I name Eric Lawrence because it is on the IEInternals blog; the page itself does not give a surname.

That the YouTube banner mostly moved home users, that IE6 Countdown's launch a year to the day after the funeral was a coincidence, and the remark about most browsers now running on Google's engine are my own inferences. I also did not open a source for Chrome's 2008 launch.

essays.title: JSConf 2009: the community that didn't know it existed
essays.description: In April 2009 about 130 people met in a hotel outside Washington for a conference about JavaScript itself. It nearly didn't happen, and its format, its side room and its name spread around the world.
unverified: Whether this was strictly the first JavaScript conference. The organizers and attendees called it that, Kevin Dangoor hedged with "possibly", and I did not search for earlier events in other countries.

The story of the mortgage-backed deposit, the drive to the hotel and the emails rests on Jan Lehnardt's 2015 speaker notes alone. Dangoor's 2010 notes confirm only that the conference was nearly cancelled and that a "sold out" notice produced a waiting list.

Who proposed taking JSConf to Europe, and when Chris Williams first raised the idea. Lehnardt and Williams each remember making the offer, and Lehnardt's 2009 post says Williams asked "last fall" while the 2015 talk places it just after RubyFringe.
The attendance figure. Dangoor wrote 130, Lehnardt "130+ attendees & speakers", and the sponsor pitch promised 125. I found no official count.
That the Ajaxian blog's founders organized The Ajax Experience. I only opened the event archive, which lists Ben Galbraith as a speaker, so the essay says no more than that.

How many editions JSConf EU held, whether JSConf US ran in every year after 2015, and who owns the JSConf name now. The sites I opened give a "10th anniversary" in 2019, a 2019 event in Carlsbad and a 2025 event "under the OpenJS Foundation", and nothing firmer.
That scarcity made community conferences harder to get into, that no library had been "the host" before, and that the job title needed the room. Those are my readings, not sourced claims.

essays.title: The blogs and the feed reader: an industry run by correspondence
essays.description: From about 2004 to 2013, front-end development argued, reviewed and patched itself across a few personal websites, and Google Reader delivered the whole exchange until Google switched it off.
unverified: Ajaxian itself. The site no longer serves its archive and I could not reach an Internet Archive copy, so its story rests on Dion Almaer's announcement, other people's mentions and an index of its titles. That its founders joined Mozilla in 2008 comes from one of those titles, not from the entry.

The inside story of Google Reader (the Fusion prototype, the 30 million peak, maintenance mode, the pope) comes from one article in The Verge, and its source for the 2013 announcement had already left Google.

The early RSS dates, the Bloglines sale, the adoption of the feed icon and GitHub's launch month come from Wikipedia. The RSS 2.0 specification's own history says August 2002 where Wikipedia says September, so I wrote only the year.
Feedly's 500,000 new users is the company's own figure, as relayed by The Next Web.

Peter-Paul Koch's 2004 article on inline event handlers is known to me only through Simon Willison's quotation of it, and Apple pointing to QuirksMode for JavaScript documentation is Koch's own account.
That links moved to Twitter, Reddit and Hacker News, that code moved from blog entries to GitHub, and the comparison of a patched blog entry to a pull request are my own readings.

essays.title: JSLint and The Good Parts: the subset that became the language
essays.description: Douglas Crockford's linter and thin book told developers which parts of JavaScript to stop using, which started a fork and a fight over a semicolon and left much of its advice inside the language.
unverified: I could not open the book itself or O'Reilly's page for it, so the publication month, the back cover text and the page numbers come from Crockford's own site and an Open Library record, and the one passage I quote from chapter 1 comes from Wikiquote.

Sources disagree on when JSLint first appeared: the Wirfs-Brock and Eich history cites its web page as 2001, while the JSHint project's history and the copyright line say 2002, and I have not seen a dated release.

The older JSLint documentation I quote is an undated copy on a university course site, and Crockford's 2001 essay is quoted from the page as it stands now, which has been revised since, so I can't say which year any particular wording dates from.

Anton Kovalyov's 2011 post is quoted from a copy in a Disqus repository because the original address no longer loads, and its quotations of Douglas Crockford and Brendan Eich are Kovalyov's attributions, which I could not trace to their origins.

That strict mode is JSLint's subset moved into the language is my own argument: the Wirfs-Brock and Eich history traces it to Crockford's recommendations to the committee and does not mention the tool. That ESLint's rule names descend from JSLint's option names, and that a frozen standard is why the subset caught on, are also my readings.

essays.title: YSlow: the letter grade that made front-end performance a job
essays.description: How a Yahoo research chart, thirteen rules and a Firebug add-on that graded pages from A to F turned page speed from a server problem into a front-end discipline.
unverified: I could not open the Internet Archive from where I was working, so I never saw the 2007 versions of Yahoo's YSlow page, its rules page or the Yahoo Developer Network release announcement; the rule text and Apache lines I quote come from the rules page as it stands now, which has been edited since.

I read the YUI Blog research articles in an archived copy hosted at derek.io, not on the original site. That copy bylines Part 1 to Tenni Theurer and Part 2 to "YUI Team"; a September 2007 YUI Blog post calls Theurer the author of the whole series.

I did not open Yahoo's own release announcement. The July 25, 2007 date comes from posts stamped that day and may be July 24 Pacific time, the OSCON link rests on two bloggers that week, and the early scores and rule weights from Simone Chiaretta are quoted from Jeff Atwood's post, not from Chiaretta's own pages.

The grading code I show is from the later open-source release, not the 2007 extension. That the E grade was added after 2007 is my inference from scores in the fifties being reported as F that summer.

I found no statement of when YSlow was last released or how long the Firefox add-on kept working; that its Firefox version ended with Firebug in 2017 is my inference, and so is the claim that these rules did more than any framework to make a build step normal.

essays.title: Cornify: unicorns on every page
essays.description: How a 2009 joke about single-feature startups put glittery unicorns on ESPN and Stack Overflow with one script tag, a bookmarklet and a Konami-code snippet.
unverified: I could not open the Internet Archive's 2009 captures of cornify.com or its script, so my account of the original code rests on the copy committed to GitHub in April 2011 and on what people described in 2009.

The history of the wrappers around the script is thin: I found Paul Irish's snippet, John Hobbs's Unicorn Blitz and a 2010 Hacker News thread, but no official jQuery plugin and no count of how many sites used any of them.

I found no report naming who put the unicorns on ESPN.com or confirming whose Konami code was used; that they sat there for weeks rests on one line in Paul Irish's post, The Register later dated the prank to April Fools' Day, and my suggestion that ESPN's wrapper called the script several times is a guess from how the reports describe it.

I name Christoph Ono only from the GitHub profile of the account that maintains the repository, which links to the studio in Cornify's footer; the Cornify site and its Hacker News account never give a person's name.

The claim that Cornify began as a spoof of single-feature startups comes from the user-written Know Your Meme entry, Stack Overflow's 2009 joke is known to me only from the company's 2010 blog post, and my guess that the url parameter fed the home-page counter is an inference from the code.

essays.title: Annex B: the features the web kept
essays.description: The JavaScript standard keeps escape(), substr, "text".blink() and HTML comments in an appendix of things it would delete if it could, and that appendix went from optional advice in 1999 to a requirement for every browser.
unverified: I read Netscape's early JavaScript reference in a mirrored copy on a university server, because the Internet Archive would not open for me. The mirror carries no date, and I placed it in the Navigator 3 era from its "Implemented in Navigator 3.0" entries.

The "icky" classification of __proto__ and the remark that the committee agreed to move syntax items into the main body come from comments on two GitHub pull requests, which I read through an automated page summary and not line by line.

That the unescape(encodeURIComponent()) trick became a familiar way to feed btoa(), that it helps keep escape() from being removed, and that it accounts for a fair share of today's escape() calls are my own impressions. I have one 2006 blog post for the trick and no usage figures.

The third edition gives no reason for moving escape() to the annex. Tying it to the function's handling of Unicode is my reading, and the "C++" search-box example is my illustration, not a documented incident.
The history paper says substr was "moved" to Annex B in 1999. I found no mention of it in the first or second edition, so I say the annex was its way into the standard.

essays.title: Wat: the jokes about [] + {}
essays.description: Gary Bernhardt's four-minute talk "Wat" and the wtfjs site turned JavaScript's type conversions into a running joke, and every punchline, from [] + {} to a line that only works because {} is parsed as a block, is the specification doing what it says.
unverified: I did not watch the video of "Wat": I quote it from the caption file on its own page, which has transcription slips, and I take what appeared on screen, the jsc console and the exact " Batman!" line from the Stack Overflow question and Hacker News comments written that week.
I date the talk to January 2012 from the conference's name and from write-ups and Hacker News submissions dated January 18 to 28; I found no page giving the day it was delivered.

That wtfjs began in February 2010 rests on the dates of its oldest posts and its own about page; I never saw the original Tumblr site, "about 120 posts" and "dozens of contributors" are my counts from the repository, and that Brian LeRoux spoke on PhoneGap at the first JSConf rests on the JSConf essay in this collection, not on a source I opened for this one.

Stack Overflow and GitHub refused my direct requests, so I read the question and answer through the Stack Exchange API and the repositories as clones; the vote and point counts are what those services reported on the day I looked.

Three claims are my own inference: that the missing try statement helps explain why + returns a string, that making Symbol and BigInt throw was the committee's answer to the coercion jokes, and that JSFuck's practical use is evading filters. I did not open the Sla.ckers.org discussion JSFuck credits, and I found no first author for the banana joke beyond what Denys Dovhan's list says.

essays.title: #!: the URLs no server ever saw
essays.description: From 2010 Twitter and then Gawker put their pages behind twitter.com/#!/name addresses that only JavaScript could read, and the outage and argument that followed sent rendering back to the server.
unverified: Twitter's 2012 engineering post "Improving performance on twitter.com" would not load for me, at its current address or in the Internet Archive copy the essay links. Its text, date and byline come from NBC News, .net magazine and The Next Web, and I could not check them against the original.
The five-hour length of the Gawker outage rests on Mike Davies's essay alone. Other writers confirm the outage, but none gives a duration, and I found no account from Gawker of what failed.

Dan Webb's tweet about undoing Twitter's hashbang URLs is known to me only through Ubergizmo's report. Webb's essay "It's About The Hashbangs" is gone from Webb's site, so I rely on other pages for its existence and title.
Ben Ward's "Hash, Bang, Wallop" would not load either. The line of Ward's I quote is an earlier remark, taken from Davies's essay and not from its original page.

I could not open Google's full crawling specification, which now redirects to a general page, so the mechanism is described from the 2009 proposal and the 2017 notice. That Twitter's seeded request cache is an ancestor of today's hydration data, and that the scheme worked as permission for new hashbang sites, are my own readings.
